utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, I would like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to wish them a Happy New Year, as I would like to wish everybody involved in this trial. I'd like to also be sure that everybody hears me. Very well. I think that each person would like to wish the other person the best wishes for our colleague who is not here today. He is still in the hospital, in fact, and we will set up a closed session as soon as we feel it is appropriate, and what we discuss during those conferences will determine what we're going to do later on. Let me first turn now to the Defence counsel and ask them what the programme or the schedule is today for hearing witnesses, for today and for the rest of the week. Perhaps there will not be any hearings on Wednesday, at least not in the morning, and that there would possibly be no hearing in the afternoon on Wednesday either, but that will still be confirmed. Mr. Hayman, do you wish to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Judge Shahabuddeen. We have a witness here today. We would like to proceed by deposition as we have in the past. In fact, our witnesses for this week are either here or are en route, and given the tickets and visas that have been obtained, we would like to proceed this week via deposition. We would like to reserve the question of next week until some further discussion with the Court is had. We don't know if we want to proceed next week or not. That does affect our disclosure obligation to the Prosecutor. If we haven't resolved that today, today is the seventh day before next Monday, so if we're going to proceed Monday, a week from today, we need to give notice to the Prosecutor of the witness or witnesses who would appear on that day. So I advise Your Honours of that scheduling deadline that we, the Defence, face. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you have any comments you want to make about what has just been said? If I've understood correctly, this will be a regular week this week, I'm saying this for the public gallery because the public gallery has to be aware of what is being done in the courtroom, but exceptionally, we could, pursuant to one of the Rules of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which says that in case one of the Judges is not available, the two other Judges may hear, in deposition form, the witnesses and then report on what they heard to their colleague. In other words, the Trial Chamber designates court officers, and that's why we're not in our robes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, counsel. Mr. President, we have no objection to proceeding by deposition. That has been our position in the past. It remains our position and will remain our position in the future. Obviously, it's important to be apprised as soon as possible of the witnesses in the future, and we would invite the Court to assist us in advancing that issue as quickly as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. First we will think about this, that is, myself with Judge Shahabuddeen. For the witnesses who are going to come now, Mr. Hayman, about how much time do you need, that is, the one who is supposed to testify this afternoon. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, about an hour and a half, two hours at the most for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which means that we could hope to finish with the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination by tomorrow morning, and if there is no hearing on Wednesday, we might have a Status Conference tomorrow afternoon, we will see as the trial proceeds, which would allow the Defence to organise itself in respect of disclosure and the notifications that it is required to provide to the Prosecutor. Judge Shahabuddeen, did you wish to say something? All right. Having said this, we will think about this issue, that is, Judge Shahabuddeen and myself, and in the meantime, we will think in light of the news that we receive from our colleague whom you know had to be operated on. Having said this, I think we can now have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, sir? Please remain standing for a few more minutes. Tell us your name, your first name, your profession, your age, where you were born, and where you reside because you are not covered by protective measures, and then you will take an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Marinko Palavra. I was born in Travnik in October 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, I was a gymnastics teacher, physical education, and at present, I work in the Federal Defence Ministry attached to the HVO, and my duties and assignments are chief of military police in the security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The usher is now going to give you the oath that you are expected to read. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated now. You have agreed to come to the Tribunal at the request of the Defence in the trial at the International Criminal Tribunal of General Blaskic, who at the time of the alleged crimes was a colonel, and he is here in this courtroom on your left. First of all, you are going to answer the questions that the Defence counsel, Mr. Nobilo, is going to ask you, and then the Prosecutor will ask you some questions, and the Judges may ask you questions as well. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Palavra, you have already said where you were born, and I'd like to ask you now, by way of an introduction, to give us a little more detail about yourself. Tell us, up until the war, which schools did you attend and what did you do until the outbreak of the war conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Please address yourself to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I went to primary school in Nova Bila. After that, I went to Travnik where I did my secondary professional training. After that, I began working in the Boris Travnik Combine as a craftsman. I was there for about one year. Then I went to join up with the former Yugoslav People's Army, and after completing my military service, I remained in Belgrad and studied at the Higher School of Pedagogy, physical culture and physical education, and I became a gymnastics teacher. Unfortunately, I was not able to continue my education because my father had seven children. I went back to Travnik and began working at the primary school there, and I worked for one year, after which I went to Han Bila, the school there, and I was also a gymnastics teacher there. For the last one and a half years, I was the director, the headmaster, of the school in Han Bila when the war broke out, and in the war, I received my assignments and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we go on to discuss the war years, may I ask you to speak as slowly as possible so that our interpreters could translate what you're saying exactly. As you've told us about working with children in primary schools as a teacher, you were also a judo competitor and a judo trainer, coach. Could you tell us a few words about that activity of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I started practicing judo in 1974, and right up until the beginning of the war, I won state medals, that is to say, the medals given for the sport by the former Yugoslavia for my category, and I was the multiple champion of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have a black belt, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. I am a black belt holder and was for many years a coach in the Nova Bila Judo Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you just mention the functions you held during the war up until the time when you were appointed commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, because your testimony will relate to the time after which you became commander. So from the beginning of the war up until the time you took over your assignments with the military police, could you tell us your duties in Travnik and where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: From the municipal command of the HVO Travnik and the commander of the Travnik brigade, the late Ivica Stojak, I was given my assignments, and I was told to set up a military police at the municipal level, and I performed this duty, that is, from April 1992 up until September 1992, I was in the military police of the HVO of Travnik. That was the municipal police. After that, I was transferred to the police station in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it's the civilian police force. I went to the Travnik police station, I was transferred there, and there I became commander of the Special Purposes Unit attached to the police station of Travnik. I performed this function up until the beginning of the conflicts between the HVO and what was, at the time, the Muslim forces in Travnik. After that, with part of the unit, I was transferred via Bukovica to the free territory of the municipality of Travnik which was controlled by members of the HVO, and I stayed there until the 1st of August, 1993. Let me mention at this point that when I came from Travnik, the unit that I commanded went in two directions, followed two directions. The wounded and, unfortunately, those who were killed remained in Travnik, and the wounded were transferred across Vlasic, and the other part of the unit went with me across Bukovica, and we were placed at the disposal of the command of the Travnik brigade of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now let's go on to the main part of your testimony. Could you explain to the Court when and how you were engaged and appointed commander of the regional military police or the 4th Battalion of the military police in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Travnik brigade, I was placed at the disposal of the commander of the Travnik brigade. My work in the Travnik brigade in the operations department was for the next two months, and then I was ordered, received orders, by the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, Colonel Blaskic, and I was ordered to be transferred to the 4th Battalion of the military police in Vitez. Prior to that, they held consultations with me in the Travnik brigade, and along with agreement from the head of the police department of Travnik allowing me to become the commander of the 4th Battalion, acquiescing, and, of course, I had to give my own agreement as well to perform this new function at the level of the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia, and, as I say, I was elected to be commander of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was this order from Colonel Blaskic? Was it standard practice? Was it usual for the commander of the Operative Zone to appoint the commander of the 4th Battalion or was this an exception? Would you explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Were there normal conditions, I would have got this order from the military police, but as it was, I was given my orders within the encirclement of Central Bosnia, the Muslim army, at a meeting in the Operative Zone. And Colonel Blaskic, with his commanders, the brigade commanders, having tried and tested me and performed this procedure, gave his agreement, and they appointed me temporarily as commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say that Blaskic appointed you temporarily, what does that mean? Were you given an order later on from your superior officer in charge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I was nominated and appointed later on. I received my nomination as commander of the 4th Battalion. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did this appointment take place? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The appointment was dated the 1st of August, 1993 which means that they confirmed my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the head of the department of the military police, where was that located?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The headquarters were located in Ljubusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is in Herzegovina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, in Herzegovina. And in view of the fact that there was no physical link between the units, we remained detached in the territory of Central Bosnia so that the rules governing the military police, the most responsible individual in the zone of responsibility was the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We'll say a little more about that later on. Tell us now, please, we have to wait for the interpretation, when you agreed to take up your duties as commander of the military police, can you describe to me your first contacts with Colonel Blaskic? What did he tell you, what did he expect you to do, and why did the subsequent changes take place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In the Travnik brigade, workers came from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. They came to the Travnik brigade, and this was under the command of Colonel Blaskic. And I remember that this operations officer in charge of personnel came and told me that I had been elected to be appointed commander of the 4th Battalion, that I had passed all the tests necessary for this post, and that Colonel Blaskic had sent them to come to me to see if I, myself, agreed to the new appointment. Of course, I was told the situation, described the situation, and I accepted the appointment. So with my agreement, after having agreed, I went to the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that is to say, to Colonel Blaskic himself. I was received by Colonel Blaskic. I was received by him. It was a sort of initial meeting to get to know each other, and at that meeting, I was surprised because Colonel Blaskic congratulated me straight away on my new appointment, and I quote, he said, "I congratulate you. You have temporarily become a commander of the 4th Battalion. You have the most responsible task to perform, the most responsible function in the Operative Zone." I was not even aware of the actual words he said on the occasion, and that's what the working meeting with Colonel Blaskic was like to begin with. In the beginning, Colonel Blaskic gave me his vision or a cross-section of the existing state of affairs in the military police force and gave me his vision of what he would like the military police to be, how he saw it, and this was reflected in the following activities: First of all, he said that he was not satisfied with the state of affairs within the military police in Central Bosnia and that the military police must, in the shortest space of time possible, become reintegrated. Furthermore, he said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: That the military police must be a popular police force, and that meant that in the area controlled by the HVO, it must not view only one side and one nation. It must be a completely national police force because in the Lasva Valley, there were the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims, and the rest, and, therefore, the military police must work according to the letter of the law and according to its competencies and authorisations and that there were no Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, but that it must protect the property of one and all, of all the people living on the territory of Central Bosnia, regardless of ethnicity. At the same time, Colonel Blaskic said that the military police must be a regional police force in the true sense of the word because the situation as it was was not a satisfactory one which means that the military policemen and in the military police, that there must be enough room for everyone, for the people of Travnik, officers from Travnik, officers from Kakanj, from Jajce, and for everyone. At the same time, Colonel Blaskic said that in the military police force, there were a certain number, a considerable number, of military policemen who did not fulfil their code of conduct as policemen and that they must, as soon as possible, get rid of people like that, of individuals like that. And I remember him emphasising the fact that in our region, that is to say, in the Lasva River Valley, there were units from different countries of Europe and the world who had come there on assignment. They did not come of their own free will but they came to fulfil a set assignment. And at that time, UNPROFOR was stationed there and various other international organisations such as the UNHCR, the Red Cross, and the European Monitors, they were all present. And Colonel Blaskic said that the military police must and that it was its task and duty to do so, that is to say, to protect both property and the lives of people living in the region because they were doing their job ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I think that there was -- that something was not quite clear in the interpretation. When he said that you should protect, did he have in mind the international organisations you mentioned, the Red Cross, the UNHCR, the European monitors and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. He emphasised that in our region, there were organisations of this kind, such as UNPROFOR, the various humanitarian organisations, the UNHCR, the European monitors, and it was our duty at all times to protect those people because there were cases where people had some troubles and problems, so that we had to protect the property and lives of those people. That was our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when he talked to you about regional representation for the military policemen, did he indicate the command, in particular?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I did not have time to say that. He said that I must pay attention to true regional representation for everyone in all the brigades that were active in Central Bosnia, that is to say, the military police must be composed of members of all the brigades, especially the command of the 4th Battalion. There were about 70 per cent -- 70 per cent represented cadres from Busovaca and that that was not how it should be and that there should be reorganisation in the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Blaskic explain why it was important to have a balance and equal representation from all the brigades and all parts of the Lasva enclave? Why was this important?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, he did explain why this was important. He said that in the military police, and I saw for myself on the spot that the situation was like that, there was a certain amount of what I would call localism on the part of the military policemen so that they were linked to their own localities, their places of residence, where they lived and worked, and that's how they had behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What you want to say is that they were lenient towards their relatives and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. Giving the answer to the witness before the question is asked or in the question isn't proper, Mr. President, so I would just ask that in the form of the question, counsel ask the question as opposed to providing the answer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, in general, that would be a better thing to do, but this was not really very serious. The witness is one of those witnesses who really knows why he came to testify, but having said this, it is true that it would be better if you were to try not to influence the witness, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. I just tried to speed things up a bit, but there's no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I knew that you were going to say that to me, Mr. Nobilo. I knew you were going to say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We've known each other for too long now. I think we should get this trial over with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. All right. Ask your question properly and don't try to suggest the answer to the witness. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you use the expression "localism," what do you mean or what did Colonel Blaskic mean when saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Localism, at that time, well, quite a few people were brought in. Quite a few people were brought in by the military police. And some were brought in, others were not brought in. They would not bring in people who were their friends or neighbours, so certain assignments were not carried out right, so an attempt was made to reorganise the military police, to have people from all regions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you're saying "brought in," you're trying to say brought into custody?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, brought into custody, people who had committed crimes allegedly or, rather, being taken to a military investigation prison, and disciplinary measures were not really taken by commanders, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Blaskic mention some other things to you that you would have to do during a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, yes, you interrupted me really. Colonel Blaskic also said that one had to go to the military police units to monitor what the situation actually was, that I should go and see for myself what the situation was and that I should propose certain measures or, rather, that we should try to carry out that which is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me which military police units did you have available in the Lasva River Valley? Could you please enumerate them for us?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: After the meeting, which took about 40 minutes, I went straight away to the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police. It was in the building where the civilian police of the Vitez municipality was, but it was upstairs. I called a meeting of all the commanders of the companies, and at that time, I only had under my control the Lasva River Valley where the first company of the military police was, the first active company, and also the first company of the traffic police and, naturally, the command. I omitted to mention something. Colonel Blaskic also told me at this meeting, because I had not known that before, that I would have problems with the second and third companies because there are no physical contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, from a territorial point of view, where was the second company and where was the third company and where were the companies of -- the first company, rather, and the first active company?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The first active company was in Vitez. The command of the company was at the hotel. The first company of the general military police was stationed in Nova Bila. And platoons of the general military police of the first company were in Busovaca, one platoon was there, Vitez, Nova Bila and Novi Travnik. The second company of the military police was stationed in the area of Kiseljak, that is to say in the operation zone -- I don't remember what the name was of the second group. And then there was this third company of the military police, it was, from a territorial point of view, in Zepce. The commander down there, to the best of my knowledge of the operative group, was General Ivo Lazaric, and in Kiseljak it was Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, these commanders of the second and third companies from Zepce and Kiseljak, when did you first see them physically? When did you actually meet them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I did not know the commanders of the second and third companies at all, because I was physically separated from them and there was no accessibility at all, because this entire area of Central Bosnia was fragmented. This was during the aggression, that is to say during the attack of the Muslim forces on those areas where Croats lived. And I didn't have any communications, really, except sometimes from the communication centre in Vitez I would sometimes receive reports that were sent to me by parcel from Kiseljak, and from Zepce very seldom. So as far as Kiseljak and Zepce are concerned, I first went there after the cease-fire was signed between the HVO units and the BiH Army units. That was in April, May 1994. That is the first time I saw the commanders, and I was supposed to be their superior officer, in fact. But since I was unable to command them, I -- they were subordinated to the commanders of the groups in the places I mentioned, that is to say Kiseljak and Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court, after this conversation and after you realised what the situation was in the military police and the military police units that were accessible to you personally, could you summarise the situation that you found there? What was the situation like in the military police of the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: After the meeting -- rather, after I was received by General Blaskic, at that time Colonel Blaskic, naturally I agreed with practically everything that we discussed at the Operative Zone, and I went out to carry out my tasks, and I only went to see the area of the Lasva River Valley where the headquarters actually was, that is to say the two companies were there as well. I convened a meeting of the commanders of the companies and I told them that I would call on their units and their objective was to get together as many military policemen as possible in order to have meetings with them and to set the guidelines as to what should be done in the future. Unfortunately, there were very few people who responded and who came to these meetings because the Muslim units kept attacking all the time in the area of Central Bosnia. Many people were assigned to carry out defence duty and the situation I found was as follows: A large number of military policemen were at the frontline precisely because of these attacks. Military policemen went home once a week, and this is a fact that was established, and they did that openly to take a bath, to wash up, to see their families. And the very same day they would return to their units and then they would try to get some rest there and prepare for the next shift and for going back to the frontline. There were very few military policemen who were actually doing military police work. I also established that very few military policemen did military police work precisely for the mentioned reason, that is to say because there were so many attacks in the area of Central Bosnia. I had quite a few of my men killed and also quite a few military policemen were wounded and there were new -- there were no new replacements coming in from anywhere. Simply everyone was involved. The situation in the brigades, I established that many requests that were coming in from brigade commanders that were sent to the military police were not actually met. These requests were as follows: Bringing people to the frontline, that is to say those who did not want to go to the frontline, or simply you'd have people who would leave the frontline of their own free will. Also bringing people into the military disciplinary prison. At that time that was Kaonik. That is to say that people were not brought into custody. Well, there were people brought into custody, but since the military police was operating in this local area, they simply made excuses. They said, "No, he's not at home. We'll go and look for him again." Also, I established that quite a few requests for bringing persons in that were sent by the Military Prosecutor's Office and by the Court of law were not met and carried out at all in terms of bringing in witnesses or accused persons, although at that time the Court of law, in fact in my opinion, was practically frozen. They had nothing to do because everything was subjected to the defence of this area. So practically there was a freeze on Court activities. I also established that there was no co-operation with the civilian police and that co-operation was very rare. Military policemen behaved arrogantly and in a superior way towards these civilian police. Of course, I am referring to individuals. And they would say that they were military policemen and that the civilian police had nothing to do with them, that they were the ones who were now in charge. And there were even some assaults on civilian policemen and I had to impose sanctions straight away. That is to say, I had to take disciplinary action or send people away from their units, depending on what they had actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, did you notice that persons or groups from the civilian or military police were linked to crime and the world of crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that many policemen who were in the unit were actually inclined towards crime and there were quite a few criminals in the area of Central Bosnia. So I can say, and it is general knowledge that this was the Vitezovi, the unit of Zuti, and some Skakavci grasshoppers and I don't know what all. So one had to react. I also established that poor equipment in the military police, especially the general platoon from Travnik, because everything that belonged to them remained in Travnik and they had to leave Travnik, of course, as they were protecting civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, or perhaps you could give us an example of the conjunction between your military policemen and certain crime groups or the Vitezovi, how could you see this conjunction?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In the battalion command I personally replaced the assistant commander because whatever the military police tried to plan was revealed immediately, so we could not really have any major successes that way. And, as I realised this, I tried to clear up the situation in the military police immediately. There were quite a few cases and there was quite a bit of crime. And at the meeting with Colonel Blaskic it was also mentioned that there were certain military policemen who were criminally prosecuted because they should be. And I tried to investigate this a bit and I can even give you the name of the person who was there in the command and who was sent away and proceedings were initiated against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And tell me, this case, when the assistant commander for crime activities -- when you sent him away, what is it that you actually found out? Why did he lose his post? Just a minute, please. I asked about the assistant commander for -- not for crime activities but for criminology activities, so could the transcript please -- for crime investigation activities, but that's not what was said. And could you please say what exactly he did, why did you send him away?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: We were supposed to do something in Vitez. We were supposed to get hold of certain cars that had been stolen because we realised that in front of the cafe that belonged to Darko Kraljevic there were quite a few vehicles that did not belong to them. Since my assistant commander held utmost responsibility for that, he was probably terrified of Kraljevic, and he went to the cafe and he said such and such a thing will be done at such and such a time, so nothing came out of this. And we even drunk in the cafe and he was drunk too. When he talked to me from the cafe, he addressed me and said, "Commander, don't do that now."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the punishment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: And this got me very angry, this made me very angry, and I suspended him. I suspended him straight away and I sent him away. And after that he went to work at the Defence Department in Travnik, yes, Travnik, and I don't know where he was sent after that, what units, but he was no longer assistant commander. And that's how things were done at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So are you trying to say that he became a rank and file soldier instead of being your assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You also mentioned equipment. Did you have crime investigation labs, you, the military police, in the Lasva River Valley or in the civilian police for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At that time we could only develop certain films and all other processing had to be done at military police headquarters, but at that time we did not have any experts, we did not have ordinary equipment, and what we did have was taken away when army military police units would come across this. So we could not actually carry out this kind of crime investigation processing without the help of the headquarters, the military police headquarters that was in Ljubusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And tell me, did you have a doctor, a coroner, in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I do not remember. I cannot recall anyone being there. I remember in Zenica there was Dr. Turkovic. And in that particular environment, no, we didn't have anyone, no, we didn't have anyone who could professionally do this and investigate certain crimes or, rather, the circumstances under which certain murders or whatever was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And tell me, did you have experts in ballistics or for explosive devices?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I only had a technician, a crime investigations technician, but not a real expert, no. No one was authorised for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And tell me, what about communications? What did you have as military police by way of communications?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: As far as the communications system is concerned, I found only a few Motorolas in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is a Motorola? Is that a radio station that you hold in your hand?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I also had wire communications, like a telephone, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this telephone, was it a special kind of telephone, military telephone, or was it a plain civilian telephone?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It was a civilian telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, after you realised what the situation was in the military police, what were the measures that you took in order to deal with the situation in the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: After monitoring the situation in the military police, attempts were made to improve the situation on the ground, and this can be seen in the following activities. Commanders of companies were given the following assignment, that they would have to send reports in every day to the commander of the military police battalion, and that was me at that time, and I had to know every day what was going on in the police. I agreed with Colonel Blaskic and thereafter issued an order saying that company commanders who were in areas that were covered by brigades had to attend briefings at the offices of the brigade commanders, that is to say that the military police had to be linked up with the brigade commands. Co-operation, coordination was established immediately with the civilian police too. First of all, I, as commander of the battalion, had certain meetings with the representatives of the court of law, of the military prosecutor's office, of the civilian police, and at these meetings I said that we had done such and such things and that the situation would have to be improved. Joint patrols were established, military police together with the civilian police, and they operated together, that is to say jointly. There was no more resentment or arrogance towards the civilian police. All requests that remained unresolved and that were coming in from brigade commands and headquarters, with regard to any particular matter, had to be responded to, and this pertained to various forms of assistants, also bringing people into custody, and then also when apartments had to be entered or, rather, there were military policemen who gave themselves the right to enter other people's apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were the measures that you took towards those military policemen who did not carry out their new assignments and duties?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, but I wanted to speak in a certain sequence, and I have a certain sequence in my mind and I wanted to respond in that order. Also, discipline was introduced in the military police and it consisted of the following: A person who would violate the military police Code of Conduct -- well, it depends, it depends on what he had done, but disciplinary action would be taken against him. So disciplinary action would be taken by way of punishment. And many would actually be handed over to the Department of Defence and then the Department of Defence, naturally, would assign them to certain units. They knew what they were doing. And people were brought in from units and brigades in the following way: Only those who were considered to be the best in the opinion of the commander -- commanders would be sent, but again we would check on them in the military police because I, together with my assistants, we would look at various records that we had. So although they did receive these evaluation reports from their commanders, we would look through the records and see whether they had any criminal records or anything like that. And every person who would be sent away or, rather, who would be expelled from the military police would regret it afterwards. And they would say, "Commander, please don't do this to me. I'll never do this again. Please don't send me to the units." And those who would come from units, that is to say from the brigades, their rule was -- I mean, as a rule they were good soldiers. And it was a honour for them to join the military police. So there was a kind of competition. Everybody wanted to join the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, did Blaskic personally become involved in this reorganisation of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Colonel Blaskic, at the meetings that we had with him, he said there were no problems with regard to the education and training of the military police, that he would help us there. And after I had informed him of the situation and had sized up the situation myself, taken stock of it, I would inform Colonel Blaskic. He was in the Operative Zone at the time located in Vitez, and I would go there daily, every morning for our briefings. I would go to Colonel Blaskic. And quite normally we would tender our reports regarding the situation in the unit, what had been done, what was to be done in future, and I would take over the tasks given me, the assignments given me by the commander of the Operative Zone for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, did he visit the units with you or did everything take place at the morning briefings?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: After I had taken stock of the situation and told him of the measures I intended to take, Colonel Blaskic agreed with what I had proposed and he insisted and ordered, in fact; that is, he said he himself wished to visit the military police units. So that we knew exactly on what day and at what time Colonel Blaskic was at the first company and the other platoons. And we would give them the order to organise ourselves accordingly to prepare for Colonel Blaskic's visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Of course, after this had taken place, we would talk to the military policemen and their commanders, we would discuss the situation in the units at the time. And we did not have any electricity at that time, so that the public information media, that is to say nobody listened much to them or watched television or anything of that sort. And Colonel Blaskic at these meetings would briefly explain the military and political situation and the situation as it existed at that moment, the tasks of the military police, what the situation was beforehand, what the present situation was, and he would congratulate them on a job well done. And at the time he congratulated the members of the military police, so he was probably satisfied with the set-up and work of the military police, and he wanted to give them public recognition for this and congratulate them in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This reorganisation and this new model of work, did it bear fruit outside the Operative Zone? Did they congratulate you outside the Operative Zone at the end of 1993? What was the quality of your military police unit considered to be like?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At that time the 4th Battalion of the military police became the best unit in the -- attached to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and we have this in writing, this commendation in writing from Colonel Blaskic, commander of the Operative Zone. And I received congratulations in writing as well, as commander of the battalion, and many military policemen were congratulated and received this -- these letters of merit. And by linking us up with the military police department and when we went off, he showed that we truly were the best unit of the military police within the composition of Herceg-Bosna as it existed at the time. There were four battalions at the time, four military police battalions, and we were considered to be the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, how much time you needed to take stock of the situation and to perform the reorganisation you described? You took over command on the 1st of August 1993. How long did you need to carry out all of this work and to establish along new lines the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I needed two to three months to put this through. I did not need more than that. It was very difficult at the beginning and I remember my military policemen, the men I worked with, they did not see me on one particular occasion. And when I would perform my visits and tours, they would discuss the situation amongst themselves and they said, "What do we need all this for? Why should we quarrel amongst ourselves and take each other into custody? We should kill him." And then I would turn up. They would see me. And there would be silence and nothing more would be heard. So these discussions were behind my back. But, in fact, what happened was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said you needed two to three months to translate the reorganisation into practice, but could you tell the Court how many military policemen you had at your disposal in numerical terms in the Lasva River Valley or an approximate figure, if you can give us that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At the time, I had somewhere around 220 policemen, approximately, in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like a document to be handed around, a diagram.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D497.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something with regard to the use of the military police. Could you describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the competence and how the military police was used when the system functions normally and in extraordinary situations when the military police force is found cut off from its headquarters, the headquarters and command of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In a situation when the military police finds itself in an encirclement and the impossibility of communicating with the headquarters, police headquarters, the military police is subjugated to the command of the Operative Zone, that is to say, the commander of the collective area. Under normal conditions, that is to say, when there is communication and physical communication as well, it would function in that way. For combat activities, if the units need to be used for combat activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. May we have the ELMO switched on, and then you can use the pointer to point out how orders are issued when the military police are used for combat purposes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The orders are issued --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Under normal conditions when combat commands are issued, the commander of the Operative Zone or collective area seeks a request from the main commander for the use of the military police for combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you show us the Operative Zone, please, and then the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Here we have the headquarters, the main staff, and the commander of the main staff then continues on to the defence department, the department of defence, and the department of defence gives orders to the military police, that is to say, the minister is in charge of issuing orders for the use of the military police, and that means that the defence department issues orders to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have in mind the --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: And the military police issues its orders to regulate matters downwards, further on towards the battalion, so that the military police and that department issues orders, and the minister decides. The defence minister makes all the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To make matters clearer, let us take an abstract example. For example, if Colonel Blaskic wishes the military police unit of 50 men to attack, for example, Krcevine tomorrow at 5.00 a.m., what would he have to do?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Under normal conditions, he would have to send a request to the military police and the commander of the main staff, and the main staff would do the same. It would follow down towards the defence department and the military police. The military police would then -- that is to say, the head office for the military police would issue orders to the commander of the 4th Battalion, that is to say, to myself, that we are placed at the disposal of the commander of the main command, and nobody else would be able to command that unit, apart from the commander of the police appointed by the battalion commander, if we're talking about a platoon or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, if the minister and the head office of the military police did not agree, could Blaskic use a unit of the military police for combat activities if they disagreed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If the minister or the person in charge of the department of defence and the head office of the military police did not agree with Blaskic's proposal as to the use of the military police, would Blaskic, without their agreement, be able to use the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, he would not be able to, but the minister is there to command the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, you said that. You said that the head office of the military police commands the military police units. Now, what does this encompass? What areas does the head office of the military police cover?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The rules governing the organisation and work of the military police state that in order to perform our military police duties, we are daily responsible in concrete terms to the Operative Zone, and hierarchially speaking, up towards the head office of the military police, so the cadres, the selection of cadres, their equipment, logistics, and everything else. Education and training, the crimes investigation department, and any other work, investigation and so on, would be controlled and under the competency of the head office of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I'd like to know whether you still have many questions that you want to ask during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President, so we could take a break perhaps here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We stopped at the functions of the military police with respect to the battalion. You mentioned crime investigation. Now, did the military commander, for example, Colonel Blaskic, could he give orders to the military police as to how to investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, he could not. He could only, he or any other commander, brigade commander, or civilian could only say something or say what they know, but the crime investigation department was independent of everything else, and it was a professional department and capacitated for the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the military court and the military prosecutor's office, could it issue orders to the military police and give instructions as to what to --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The courts of law could and so could the military prosecutor. They could issue orders and did issue orders for taking individuals into custody, and I mentioned this in my testimony. They could issue orders for arrests according to their competencies and authorisation. We would then be given an order and proceed according to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what about the prosecutor's office, could it issue a demand for you to collect information and question an individual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it could, and we did do that following orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, when there was no encirclement in Central Bosnia, did you receive orders from the head office of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were not in the encirclement, let us say in 1994, for example, when communications were established, did you receive orders from the head office of the military police in Ljubusko?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: When everything began to function again, we normally became part and parcel of the system of the military police, and all orders did go from the head office, directly from the chief of the head office of the military police at the time, so that when times were normal, we were under the command -- militarily and politically, we were under their command, and military duties and police duties included arrests, taking individuals into custody, setting up controlled checkpoints. We guided convoys, escorted convoys, and so on, so we did do things of that kind for the brigades at the request and on orders that came to us from the command, whereas for everything else, we were under the head office of the military police, starting out from cadres' policies, the selection of cadres, equipment, military police work, and everything that the military police force does. All of this was under the head office of the military police, cadres, education and training, equipment, and so on, and those were our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the break, you mentioned a term -- you referred to the daily use of the military police. What you have just described to us, that the commander of the Vitez command could use the military police, does that come under daily use of the military police, that term?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, but once again, he had to issue a request to me as the commander, and then following on from that request, I would send the military policemen, and the heads of my platoons or companies would go on assignment following that request for order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, 1993, you became the commander and replaced the commander of the 4th Military Battalion, Pasko Ljubicic who was the commander at that time. Did you ask yourself ever why you had replaced him, why this replacement took place, and where the problem lay?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, quite normally, I did ask myself that because when I came to the command of the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia, I was told straight away what the military police did, that he was dissatisfied with the military police as it stood with the situation as it existed, and that he expected it to be transformed in all areas of work, and I came to realise that there must have been something wrong. I asked around and became informed by the unit itself, and I heard that there was a sort of feedback mechanism between Colonel Blaskic and Pasko as regards the command, because the military police, while a communications existed -- before they had been severed, they commanded the military police via the head of the military police. So the situation, however, in the Lasva River Valley and Central Bosnia was under war operations, and it was impossible to communicate with the command, and quite normally, the senior commander was to be adhered to, and the commander -- this was the commander of the Operative Zone. He was the senior commander, and that was Colonel Blaskic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you were understood and that the interpretation was correct. What happened between Pasko Ljubicic and Colonel Blaskic? What happened between the two?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know what happened between the two, but Pasko wanted to retain the hierarchy, to retain his command over the military police and did not, in fact, follow orders. Allegedly, it was the head office of the military police whose job it was to issue orders of that kind, but what I heard from various discussions with the military policemen, I found out that when I came to head the 4th Military Police Battalion, I knew that I had no communications with the head office of the military police and that I had to share the fate of the commander of the Operative Zone and of the people, and so I was in a position to command the unit while we were in the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did Pasko, just like you, carry out Colonel Blaskic's orders without questioning them at all or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, it's the best for you to ask Colonel Blaskic that. But I know there were certain complications and that Colonel Blaskic was not pleased with Pasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You became commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, and Pasko Ljubicic held that post before that, and which post did he get then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At that time Pasko got the following post -- rather, since the 4th military police battalion was cut off from the head office, headquarters, and not only them, he became assistant head of the head office of military security in Central Bosnia. This was in two months, I believe. And all orders, at first, only at the beginning, I received from Pasko, because Pasko first attended meetings with the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. And then we, in the 4th Battalion of the military police, received our orders from him, and this lasted very -- for a very short time. Then Pasko took a helicopter and went to Herzegovina to the head office of the military police. And from then onwards I took over all these posts in the 4th Battalion and I was responsible to the Operative Zone. I know that Pasko was also in charge of the 3rd Light Battalion military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As regards the 3rd Light Battalion of the military police, I would like to ask you something else; namely, in addition to the 4th Battalion of the military police there was -- there was a Light Battalion of the military police which was created out of the Jokers; is that correct? Is that correct? The Jokers were first called the Jokers and then, as things developed, this unit was renamed the Light Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I know that after I came to the 4th Battalion of the military police in Vitez that there was this 3rd Light Battalion of the military police, and it is true that it did consist of parts of the Jokers, but it was not only them. There were people from other units too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many men did this unit have?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know how many men it had, but I know that there were lists, and they reached me afterwards because the head of the military police had ordered that all lists should be submitted to the 4th Battalion or, rather, the commander of the 4th Battalion, and that was me. And at that time the 3rd Light Battalion that was in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Central Bosnia was abolished and it grew into something else, of course, under orders of the main staff. They grew into -- they were abolished, that's what I was saying, and they grew into new brigades. Quite a few of them went to these guard brigades, as they were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go back to your beginning, in 1993, that is to say when there was this Light Battalion of the military police which grew out of the Jokers as things developed. At that time you became commander instead of Pasko, and did you also take control over the Light Battalion or rather the Jokers at one point in time? Did you take over that command from Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: While Pasko Ljubicic was there, no, I did not, because he was their commander, and I did not issue a single order to the 3rd Light Battalion. Simply, they were not under my command, and that is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say that they were not under your command, that they were under Pasko Ljubicic -- I'll rephrase it. Sorry. What is this post that Pasko held in order to be able to give them orders? On behalf of what authority did he command the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: As I said, he was appointed assistant commander of the military police for Central Bosnia and he was assistant head for the military police, and Pasko commanded the 4th Battalion and the 3rd Light Battalion, but at that time I did what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So can you tell us exactly what is the exact authority of the military police that made Pasko in charge of the Jokers, that is to say the head office of the military police. One of the major problems that you encountered in your work were different groups of criminals or different units in which there were elements of crime. So could you name the two most important groups that you encountered and what was the problem between the military police and these crime groups?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, I can mention this, of course. These were units of the Vitezovi and units of the Zuti. As regards the Vitezovi, quite a few of them were at the frontline and they carried out their duties, but some of them were in a privileged position, about 15 or 20 percent of them. They did what they did, that is to say that they did not go to the frontline. They stayed at various places and they were wheeling and dealing. And also the Zuti resorted to similar things, even while there was heaviest fighting and war in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this reorganisation of yours, of the military police, what is your opinion, what is your assessment? The military police that you saw, that you took over, before your time was it in a position to actually deal with these criminal groups, with the Zuti, with the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. I said what the situation was like on the ground. Quite a few policemen were related to these criminals. They were their relatives, and also a certain number of military policemen were also involved in various criminal activities with these people from the units of Zuti and Kraljevic's units. So I'm not sure, but you saw that the military police spent more time at the frontline than carrying out their actual duties. That is what the situation was like at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At one point in time, at the end of 1993, with your unit of military police you actually had a military showdown with the Zuti. Could you please describe how this happened and what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. At that time the commander of a special unit was killed. Zoran Tuka was his name. And this commander was popular with the men in his unit and with the population in general, and intelligence reports came in saying that Tuka was killed by members of the Zuti. Because before the killing, Zoran Tuka had been wounded or, rather, he had wounded Zuti in Novi Travnik in front of a cafe, and the reaction of the Zuti people was that they killed the late Tuka, the commander who was so popular among the men in his unit, and not only among the men in his own unit. And that is when another member of the Munja unit was heavily wounded, badly wounded. And our estimate was that there would have been an escalation. Actually, that was Colonel Blaskic's assessment, that there would be an escalation between the two units, and probably there would be killings on both sides. So we took action promptly. The military police was charged with trying to apprehend the suspects and the perpetrators of this killing. This action was carried out by the military police, a certain group together with the security service at that time, and it was completed almost successfully. Not all of them were apprehended, but it went rather well. It was a job fairly well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And was there a military showdown? Was there actual fighting between the military police and the Zuti and were there dead on their side?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was an armed conflict. Because at that time we did the relevant police work, and not to go into all of that now, but they were not at a certain place and, naturally, we split up into different groups and we tried to catch them. They were in a certain house. My deputy was in charge of a certain group. I had authorised him. And he approached this house, together with his unit, and he said, "You are surrounded. Get out. HVO military police. Get out and surrender." And since these criminals knew what was going on, they started shooting. And in what followed, two members of the Zuti were killed and one of the members of my company, and also some military policemen were captured by Zuti and his group. So it ended the way it ended. At any rate, we did carry out this action and this only worked to the advantage of the population in general and the soldiers on the frontline. And after that Zuti was no longer mentioned. Zuti was wounded. And Kraljevic didn't speak up either, so the military police took over control in this area and things were getting better and better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you did not catch everyone. Please tell the Court where did these criminals run when the HVO military police attacked? Where did they run away?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: They escaped to the territory that was under Muslim units control at that time. I don't know which way they went, but, at any rate, they went up to Pavlavica and proceeded to Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, and then they went to HVO controlled territory again. And that is where they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You already mentioned some of this, but tell us again. The Vitezovi, did this action have any effect on the Vitezovi and was it conceived with that purpose in mind, to send a message to others as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Not only to the Vitezovi. The message was supposed to go to all. I know when I was appointed commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, at that time Zuti said -- that's what I was told afterwards by all the eyewitnesses. And he said, "Well, again we are going to have a war with the military police." And they asked him why. And he said that Palavra is commander again. Again there is going to be a war. So the message was quite clear. And it was sent out to Kraljevic and everyone. Either belong to the system or there is no other way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we are going to move onto some documents, but before that -- please, perhaps it wasn't quite clear during the introduction. What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Currently, at present, I work in the Federal Ministry of Defence. I am employed there and I am head of the military police department. I think I've been quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course. But we are laymen. Does that mean that you are chief of the military police? Are you at the helm of the military police of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Exactly. But this is a temporary thing. We are to receive official appointments now, and it is not only myself but all people who are currently working in the Federal Ministry for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a series of documents. I don't want to go into the contents of the documents. They speak for themselves. These are military police documents and we just want to take advantage of the presence of this witness to confirm their authenticity. So I think we are going to move through them quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This procedure was employed, of course, with Brigadier Marin, and what results, of course, is that upon reflection of these documents there is often any number of items that should be brought to the Court's attention. And like my learned friend across the bar, we should take that advantage to ask this witness those questions once those documents are examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that Mr. Nobilo was trying to accelerate things. I think that the witness said why he was -- he was called here. If we can move things forward more quickly, all the parties in the trial would be better off. The witness has been called within the spirit of these proceedings in order to say what he has to say about very specific points. In order to go back to the issue of the documents, perhaps Mr. Nobilo could have the witness identify them, and if he has any comments to make while they are being authenticated, he can do so, question the witness, but we -- I would ask you to try to move along a little more quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the idea was the following, that this witness should not speak about these documents, only confirm their authenticity. We have a similar situation when the Prosecutor brought several volumes of documents without any witnesses and tendered them, and that is the same thing we want to do. We just want this witness to confirm that these are authentic documents. We are not going to put a single question to him in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, if counsel wants to proceed in that fashion, I mean, the Prosecutor certainly has no objection. I just bring to light the fact that upon reflection of these documents it could very well be that there is -- there are matters or there is a matter within a particular document which the Prosecutor wants to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you seen the documents, Mr. Kehoe? Have you already reviewed them? Have you received them already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a translation problem. You say after review of the documents, perhaps there would be some mistakes -- you are talking about the documents having to do with General Marin's testimony? It had to do with General Marin's testimony; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened during General Marin's testimony is we went through some 210 documents and counsel would maybe talk about a sentence, and in a couple of instances there was no discussion about the document at all, and Brigadier Marin simply authenticated the document. What we discovered, upon reflection of those documents, was there was a significant amount of information, of which Brigadier Marin had knowledge that merited exploration during cross-examination. I simply raise that, and there is certainly no objection on the part of the Prosecutor to allowing the defence counsel to employ any methodology he so chooses. In any event, upon reflection what we have discovered is there are significant amounts of material in these documents which we may very well want to ask Mr. Palavra about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. If you have questions, you will ask them at the proper time. We can have the witness brought back. I don't hope to do so. I hope we can move forward quickly. Each party has used these proceedings at different points. We are professional judges, you have the documents identified and then they will be given to the judges. If, during the cross-examination, you believe that you have some comments to make, you will make them, and if at the end -- during your final arguments you have some, you can make them, but if you feel that you can't, we can have the witness brought back. Of course, I don't want that. The judges will be here also to review them. For the time being let me note that you agree to the methodology. All right. Let's move forward without any further ado with the identification of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't think the Court need be concerned. There are only 15 documents. This is not voluminous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The judges are not concerned. Let me point that out to you. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, then, I would like to ask that the witness be given the documents one by one, and if he can, on the basis of the signature and stamp, identify each document. And as head of the examination in chief, I am not going to put any questions related to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document is D498.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Palavra, the document came into being before you arrived on the scene. Would you just look at the signature. Do you recognise it, the signature at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. And it is signed by Pasko Ljubicic and it is identical to his signature. I took my orders from him. It is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D499.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is D499, which you have in your hands. Would you take a look at the signature and tell us if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the same thing. Yes, I recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. It is the administration of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D500.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have before you document D500. Do you recognise the stamp and signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Lastro is?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Zeljko Lastro was assistant for -- I didn't get the duties. When I suspended Ivan Josipovic and Lastro came to head the department for the crime -- the crime investigation department of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D501.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at document D501, please, and tell us if you recognise the signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 502.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have before you document D502. Do you recognise the signature of Zvonko Vukovic and the stamp of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And Zvonko Vukovic was in the Operative Zone and the command. He was an assistant for personnel matters and cadres matters, so we cooperated closely.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D503.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at document 503, please. Do you recognise the signature of Pasko Ljubicic and the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 504.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Document 504 is before you. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was not signed by Pasko Ljubicic but by Marijan, also a worker, an official of the military police. Yes, that's correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Marijan Jukic at the time was an assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are speaking of 504 here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, we are, D504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a version which is signed Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. Pasko Ljubicic is typewritten, but instead of him Marijan Jukic signed the document, so the signature is that of Marijan. Whereas the typewriter says Pasko Ljubicic, he was assistant for crimes, crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 505.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signed the document on the right-hand side on behalf of the military police? The document is D505.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In my opinion, this was signed by Majdancic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D506.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
