utterances.text: Therefore, document 506 was signed by Pasko Ljubicic, once again. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D507.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at document 507, please, and tell us who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Vlado Santic signed it, and he was my deputy for 15 days at one point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D508.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at document 508, please. Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Pasko signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have before you document D509. Do you recognise the stamp and signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. The signature is the administration of the military police, and it was signed by Marijan Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But who did he sign instead of?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It says, "Commander Pasko Ljubicic," but the signature is Marijan's.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D510.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Take a look at document 510, D510, and see who signed it. Look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Marijan Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Look at this document carefully, because when it was photocopied, the signature is only partially visible, so tell us what you think. Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: This was signed by Pasko. I know his writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would now like to show the witness five documents which we admitted previously. Four of them are confidential in nature, so we're going to use the witness to identify the signatures without going into the contents, and as the documents are confidential, it would be a good idea to explain to the witness what that means. So if he sees the contents or the partial contents of the document, he should know that it must remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're simply not going to put these documents on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They are D90, D91, D94, D151, and D410.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As regards D90, D91, and D94, the three documents were admitted. Document 151 has not been admitted for now, nor has 410, that is, not admitted for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: First of all, show all the documents, but the last one, D410, keep that. So show the first four documents to the witness, please, the first four documents, and D410, you keep it for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when you have taken a look at all four documents, tell us if you recognise the signatures?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The first document is all right. It is signed by Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The second document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The same goes for the second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have D90, that was Vladimir Santic. D91, who signed that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It was also signed by Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. D94, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, Marijan Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. D151, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it is the signature of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. D410, look at the signature, but don't tell us the name of the individual because the document is under seal, so it is a secret document. Just tell us whether you recognise the signature on document D410. The signature is on the first page. And the text, the title, does it correspond to the function that the individual had at the time, but don't tell us the function or the institution, just, according to the best of your knowledge, did that individual perform that function?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, he was the most responsible individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President. We have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suggest that we take our second break, since we have a very busy day. Mr. Prosecutor, would you like us to take a 30-minute break which would allow you to have some time in order to look at those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then we will resume at 5.30 for only half an hour, but that will allow you to become more familiar with the documents. All right. We will suspend the hearing until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Palavra. Mr. Palavra, we haven't met. My name is Greg Kehoe. I'm a member of the Office of the Prosecutor. The gentleman to my right is Mark Harmon, also of the Office of the Prosecutor, and to his right is Mr. Andrew Cayley, likewise, of the Office of the Prosecutor. Welcome, sir. Mr. Palavra, you told us that your current position is essentially chief of the military police in Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. At present, I'm in the Federal Ministry of Defence, and its seat is in Sarajevo, and that is where I am chief of the military police or, rather, the intelligence service which is part of the general security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pardon me. In asking this question, it's just by way of clarification, sir. Do you carry a rank now, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: At present, all the officials in the Ministry of Defence have their ranks frozen, but now a new setup is being made in the Ministry of Defence itself, and certain departments or, rather, certain heads of departments are going to be military men. They are going to hold their ranks, whereas the majority will not. Assistant ministers and the minister, of course, are civilians, but there are going to be some departments within the ministry that will be headed by persons who will be military men, and this is being agreed upon right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have a rank at this point, sir, or did you have a rank in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Colonel. While I commanded the battalion, I was a major, and after that, I became a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You carry the rank of colonel now, so if I call you "Colonel," it would be proper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's take it back to the period of time that you were in charge of the 4th Military Police Battalion in Vitez. You told us that you took that over on 1 August, 1993. Can you tell us about your career after that time up until the position that you hold right now? Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: When I took over the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police until I went to Sarajevo, that is, the 27th of August -- yes, August -- 1997, I went to the Ministry of Defence. From the 1st of August, 1993 until the 27th of August, '97, I was commander of the battalion of the military police, and at the present, I'm working in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Thank you. If we can turn our attention, if you will, to Defence Exhibit 497. Mr. Dubuisson, it's this particular exhibit, if we could place that on the ELMO. Now, Colonel, before we go into this, you did your military service in the JNA, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the former JNA, 1978/1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, in the former JNA. What role did you have in the former JNA in 1978 and 1979?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to this particular exhibit, Colonel, 497, and you noted that in normal circumstances, if you can just turn to this exhibit, if Blaskic wanted to give a combat order to the military police, he would have to send that order to the HVO headquarters in Mostar. The HVO headquarters in Mostar would then have to send that order to the Department of Defence. Assuming the Department of Defence agreed, that particular order would then be sent down to the head office for the military police in Mostar, and then that particular order would be transferred to the 4th Military Police Battalion and yourself; is that right? Is that how this transpired in normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, under normal circumstances, that's the way it should be. Then the commander of the military police, of the general office of the military police, when he would receive orders from the Department of Defence, from the assistant minister, when he would receive orders, then he would send a new order to the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police in Central Bosnia, in that particular case, myself, within the Operative Zone, that is, whoever the commander of the Operative Zone be. And not knowing what he would be using this for -- what I'm trying to say is that if I would go, for example, to Tomislavgrad, to a different area, then the head of the military police would give me orders that my military police units would be subordinated to the battalion of the military police which is currently in charge of that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you're essentially talking about a five-step process. Once Blaskic gives a combat order that he wants to bring the military police in until it gets back to you and then you make contact with Blaskic, is that right, five steps have to take place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long did that take?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know how long, but very quickly, depending on when the action was planned and depending on the commander, what he is planning, how he wants to use the units. In a military system, this works very quickly. We all know what is supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know of any other military or army in the world that operates in this fashion, the fashion that you have testified to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know of this. I just know that according to our code of the military police, I mean, that's what it says. That's the way it is. The military police and the general office of the military police is at the disposal of the Ministry of Defence, and that's the way it is. And I was one of the persons belonging to this system, so I functioned within that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, was this the system, I think you've testified to in direct examination, the system that was employed after the Washington Accords were signed in early 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any combat orders or any orders in your possession where Colonel Blaskic, who was in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone at the beginning of 1994, where Colonel Blaskic employed this particular procedure in order to order the military police into combat? Do you have any such orders, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure, sir. You testified in direct examination in response to my learned colleague, Mr. Nobilo, that this procedure that you set forth in Defence 497 was the procedure that was employed after the Washington Accords were signed in early 1994; isn't that correct? Now, Colonel Blaskic took over as the Deputy Chief of Staff in April of 1994, and my question for you, sir, is that from the time the Washington Accords were signed or, at any point, do you have any order signed by Blaskic where he employed this five-step procedure in order to order the military police into combat? Do you have any such order?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: After the cease-fire was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or at any time.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't have it here, but that was the procedure involved. The military police could have been requested by Colonel Blaskic, that is to say that he had to submit a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question for you, Colonel, is did he ever do it? Did he ever employ this five-step procedure in order to order your men from the 4th Military Police Battalion into combat? Did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has already answered this.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: But there is no problem, I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has answered it. Well, you've already said something about that question and we are wasting time now. So answer quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what the procedure is, I know what the procedure is, and I know what it's like when I receive orders, but when the Colonel or whoever addresses the head of the entire service, that I do not know. I just know when I receive my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, isn't it true that the military police, certainly the 4th Military Police Battalion, was operating on what was known as a territorial principle, and that principle was employed during the entire time you were part of the 4th Military Battalion and even before that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's a well-known thing. Wherever there were units of the Croatian Defence Council, there had to be military police units too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would you agree with the statement that in carrying out their regular duties, military police units were subordinate to the commanders of these units, HVO units, and for professional purposes to the military police administration at the Ministry of Defence for the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two questions here. Could they please be separated? The first part is one claim and in the second part is another claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I am doing, Mr. President, is reading a sentence from "The Three Years of Military Police" and an article that was written by Brigadier Zeljko Zeljek who was not in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone but I believe was in the Southern Bosnia Operative Zone, which, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know Brigadier Zeljek, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was head of the administration of military police. He was my superior officer. There is no problem. I am going to answer this question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that the military police in every area was subordinate to the Operative Zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The military police was subordinate to the commander of the Operative Zone, but only in terms of carrying out military police duties, and that is checkpoints, convoys, escorts, that is to say guarding various facilities, providing security for various facilities, however combat action, no. Not a single commander of a particular area could issue such an order without the agreement, the consent of the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, was that different from January of 1993 until the Washington Accords in 1994? In other words, could Blaskic issue combat orders directly to the military police during that time frame, January 1993 to early 1994, without consultation with Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: He could have. He could have issued such orders precisely because he was encircled and he was the only person and the most responsible person in charge of the military in Central Bosnia while it was encircled. So his responsibility was top responsibility, and naturally he acted the way he thought he should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, were you going to say something else?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So during this period of time, when the military police, as you testified, had no communications with Mostar, the military police was directly subordinate to Colonel Blaskic in all military matters as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that also includes the civilian police, as the civilian police when it came to military operations were also subordinate to Colonel Blaskic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The civilian police was subordinate to the head of the administration for civilian police, head of the police administration, and every time, as far as I know, when the civilian police were supposed to go to the frontline, because in Central Bosnia there weren't any attacks, we were defending ourselves, he would put in a request, that is to say together with the head of the police of Travnik. Then he would issue an order sending certain policemen to the frontline, that is what I know. And Colonel Blaskic at that time did not command the civilian police, although he was acting in agreement with the head of civilian police because he was the one who was in charge of sending civilian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a Defence Exhibit. Colonel, let me show you Defence Exhibit 300, if I may. Colonel, I am not sure that you have seen this particular document before. It has been received in evidence. It is an attack order issued by then Colonel Blaskic to attack on the morning of 18 April 1993 various areas in and around Kiseljak, specifically Gomionica, Svinjarevo and some other villages. And I direct your attention to paragraph 7. It says, "All army forces (military and civilian police forces) are to be placed under the command of the Kiseljak, Ban Jelacic Brigade." You can take a moment to take a look at that, sir. You will see on the following paragraph that the attack operation is to begin on the 18th of April 1993 at 0530. Now, would you agree with me, based on that, Colonel, that Colonel Blaskic, during this time frame, January 1993 to early 1994, had the power to order the military police, as well as the civilian police, into combat operations? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear, that the commander of the Operative Zone at that time was the person of utmost responsibility as regards the military, civilians and everything. So I know what the situation was in our area. In agreement with the head of civilian police, naturally policemen went to the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is this, Colonel: Would you agree, after reading that document, that Blaskic had the power to order both the military police, as well as the civilian police, into combat without consultation with anybody during this timeframe?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I would not agree with you, because we had such an army and I felt it on my very own skin. If the going is good and if you are commander, fine, but then if it's not, then you are no longer commander and that's it. And that's the way it was until the brigades were set up, everything was fine until something is needed. Then something is needed, they say, "What is this guy doing here and that doing here?" Then everybody is a wise guy. But as far as I know, there must have been consultations with the head of civilian police. I don't know. And it is Colonel Blaskic who can give the best answer to this question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you do know that that particular order, the 17th of April 1993, was issued at a time when a war was taking place in the Lasva Valley? You do know that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with that knowledge you still insist, Colonel, that Colonel Blaskic had to consult with the civilian authorities in order to send the civilian police into combat?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I gave you my answer. I don't know. You can ask Colonel Blaskic. I know what the situation was like in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, I am about to move into another area. I don't know what the schedule of the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to speak to the witness. The decision about hearing the accused is one which will be taken within a very specific procedural framework of which you are not aware, perhaps, which would be natural, and therefore I don't think that you can answer the judges -- once or twice, all right. Everybody might think that the accused has a great deal of competence in respect of answering certain questions, but there is a procedural framework here and it must be respected. Therefore, you cannot answer simply by saying, "Well, ask this one or that one." It's a very simple question and I will ask it myself. On the point 7, in order that all army forces, military and civilian police forces, are to be placed under the command of the Kiseljak, Ban Jelacic Brigade. What is your answer to that question? What is your answer? Do you contest the form of this order or -- the form of the order or the substance of the order, and if you do, would you tell us why, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In this case, in this case, orders are being given to the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade of Kiseljak by the commander of the Operative Zone. And the commanders of the operative groups in Zepce and Kiseljak, they were in their own areas the persons in charge as regards the defence of that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. No point in going any further. You've answered as you wanted to, and each party will take from what you've said what it intends to. Move to another question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you talked about this meeting that you had with General Blaskic, I believe it must have been sometime in early August 1993 or maybe the 1st of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It wasn't on the 1st of August. It was right at the beginning when I assumed this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't mean to quibble with you on the date, sir. Early August of 1993 will suffice. Now, you also noted in questions by Defence counsel that you noted that Blaskic could not tell you how to investigate a case. Do you recall that answer that you gave to Mr. Nobilo's question?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I remember. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then in this conversation that you had in early April 1993 -- excuse me, early August 1993, Blaskic noted to you that there were criminal elements not only within the military police but also the Vitezovi and Zuti, and I think you mentioned this organisation, the Grasshoppers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic have the power to order that individuals within those organisations involved in criminal activity be arrested? Did he have that power to order their arrest?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: He did have this power, but it was hearsay, this person said this and the other person said that, but investigation can only be carried out by the military police or the crime police. And on that basis the commanders of brigades and the commander of the entire area according to the information received can say, let us question this or that person, but he could not effect the actual investigation because that was done by the military police. It was only the military police that was in charge of doing this. Of course, in consultation with the Prosecutor's office and the Court. But we carried out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he have the power to tell you to arrest somebody?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, he could only say something and then the military police would resolve matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: We could -- we could call a person in to the military police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. This is an important question. The interpreters are tired. I suggest that we resume tomorrow morning about that subject. It's already ten after six. It's been a long afternoon. All right. You can re-ask your question tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning we will resume at ten o'clock. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of January, 1999 at 10.00 a.m.
